items.title: Man Creates DIY Flock-Style Cameras That Only Scan Police Plates And For Some Reason The Cops Are Annoyed By This
items.content:
Man Creates DIY Flock-Style Cameras That Only Scan Police Plates And For Some Reason The Cops Are Annoyed By This

Flock cameras , and others like them , are giving police the ability to track private citizen movements based on the vast databases of time and location data they create. For some reason, police got very concerned when YouTuber Anthony Sistilli turned the tables and made his own ALPR system that would track the police in the same way. Imagine that.

Sistilli lives in Canada, outside the reach of Flock, Axon, and other U.S. ALPR networks, reports Futurism . Yet even Canada isn't safe from this technology. Brampton, Ontario, where Sistilli lives, is the first city in Canada to adopt ALPR technology, with 360-degree cameras at 50 intersections  and in-car cameras inside  415 Peel Regional Police cruisers . While companies like Flock advertise the effectiveness of ALPRs in finding missing persons and recovering stolen cars, Brampton makes no secret that it's also  using ALPRs for parking enforcement , which is hardly a violent crime worth creating an all-seeing surveillance dragnet for. That's like using them on  garbage trucks to look for code violations .

With this technology coming to his hometown, Sistilli took an interest, and decided to see how hard it would be to build his own version. After all, if a company that makes as many huge mistakes as Flock can still be successful, how hard can it be? As it turns out, not hard at all. All he needed was an off-the-shelf camera, a laptop, and software he built using AI in about 20 minutes. His system has a twist, though. Instead of tracking everyone, as police do, he would only track police cars, turning the system around on the people who use it the most.

Sistilli released a couple of YouTube videos showing his homemade ALPR to track police cars. It wasn't actually very effective. It only correctly identified two out of seven cruisers that passed his location during the hour he tested it, and it did not capture the license plates of either one, which is about as reliable as a real Flock camera . Still, that was enough for several Peel Regional Police officers to pay Sistilli a visit about his cop-detecting ALPR, even though he'd done nothing wrong.

Only excerpts of his police encounter appear in the video, but Sistilli says that officers were very polite (I'd expect no less of Canadians ). They do appear to have a friendly chat, which is rather different than the American approach to policing . They query Sistilli about his intentions with the ALPR system. From Tom's Hardware :

One of them [the officers] took the time to specifically mention how scary it would be for them, because people would be able to find out where they lived, when they got on their shift and what they were doing throughout the day, and that that type of powerful information could put them personally at risk for any bad apples that might want to track them down.

Gee, you don't say. It's funny how the moment the cameras are turned on them, police are suddenly worried about their their own movements being tracked , and how such data could enable " bad apples " to stalk them . You know, just like police have been caught doing to innocent civilians time and time again . From Straight Arrow :

I wanted to see whether it was feasible and use the irony to illustrate a point. Sometimes it's easier to show people what this kind of surveillance means by turning it around than by simply explaining what companies like Flock are doing.

In that, Sistilli has succeeded. Yet when Sistilli pointed out the double standard at play here, the officers still didn't get it. Their failure to see the connection between their fears, and the fears of every innocent person whose license plate ends up in an ALPR database somewhere, is a whole other problem.

items.title: Context Inertia: When Agents Won’t Let Go
items.content:
Context Inertia: When Agents Won’t Let Go

Persistent models have a persistence problem.

It’s been a bit since we’ve added a new context failure mode , but the increasing persistence of frontier models has brought this fail to the fore. This one I call Context Inertia :

Context Inertia is when the model commits to a hypothesis, subtask, or goal in its context and keeps pursuing it after the evidence says to stop or change course.

This failure mode is part context poisoning (when an error makes it into the context and is repeatedly referenced) and part context distraction (when a context grows so long the model over-focuses on it), amplified by frontier models the labs have trained to be relentless instruction followers .

A couple days ago, buried in a piece about AI self-replication capabilities , Anthropic shared a perfect Context Inertia case study when describing a custom harness:

Memento is designed to mitigate a common failure mode we observe in long-horizon runs: an agent can become fixated on an incorrect idea (for, say, why a bug is occurring) and continue pursuing it instead of backtracking. One example of such a failure is a Qwen agent debugging package versioning for hours when the real bug came from implementing an endpoint incompatible with the grader API.

Each Memento agent works until a fixed timeout (1.5 hours, in one experiment), then writes a short note detailing its work. A fresh agent inherits the codebase, the environment, the note, and nothing else.

Guy Pearce as Qwen, trying to remember how to install llama.cpp.

Anthropic isn’t the only one facing this problem, or applying the forgetting fix. In just a week, we had two papers hitting exactly the same note. Jack Ziyang Cai and Christos Ziakas submitted a paper on October 5th called “ Fork-and-Flush ”, writing ( emphasis mine ):

We first examine how solution quality evolves over long autoresearch runs. The score of the best solution found so far tends to plateau within a run. More revealingly, independent runs of the same agent on the same task plateau at substantially different levels, with gaps that persist even after considerable additional compute .

When agents found good solutions, they tended to fixate on them. Better solutions existed, but the path to them was never explored. Cai and Ziakas’ baseline runs delivered a wide range of results, between 68.3 and 100.0 on one task, despite plateauing with plenty of compute budget left.

Qizheng Zhang and coauthors published a paper, “ Stateless Language Agents ” (SLAs), detailing how long-running auto-research loops settle into busy work once a sufficient solution is found. A model using the CORAL harness found its last improvement in 231 million tokens, and then just kinda…dawdled. Of the final 1,500 turns, 98% made no tool calls . The model just chewed on its existing context.

…And then, this morning , we have a fourth example: a UC Berkeley and Stanford team led by Shangyin Tan published “ Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting ”. They ran autoresearch agents three ways and all plateaued for the same reason: “Each agent became anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits.”

Tan’s solution is similar: a harness that forgets , wiping the slate and only retaining the best solution as files in the environment. Stalled autoresearch runs that could forget gained 4.5% to 9.2% over the next 30 proposals. Runs that couldn’t forget gained less than 2%, at up to twice the cost. The plots tells the story:

The y-axis is the AtCoder Heuristic Contest 014 score.

In 10 days, 4 teams running long-horizon tasks with GPT, Claude, Qwen, GLM, and DeepSeek all reached the same fix: throw the context away and keep the work.

Since writing about Context Distraction way back in June of 2025, there’s been some great research illustrating the issue. Carolina Camassa and Derek Shiller’s paper “ Do as I say, Not as I Do ” illustrates the problem rather well.

items.title: NY announces game ownership bill requiring ownership rather than licensing
items.content:
Rep. Ritchie Torres of New York's 15th congressional district has introduced the Power To The Players Act . This new legislation aims to protect consumers by directing the FTC to establish regulations on game ownership to curb anti-consumer business practices. "Under the bill, buying a video game would give the consumer ownership of the game rather than a license to play it," the release says. "Games with online functionality would also be required to provide an offline mode before the servers supporting them are shut down."

Games having an expiration date despite being more expensive than ever has been scrutinized by players all over the world, along with aggressive monetization schemes within the games themselves. Rep. Ritchie Torres isn’t the first to fight for gamers, as Pennsylvania state senator John Kane also recently introduced the Protect Our Games Act , requiring publishers to provide an offline mode, community servers, or a 25% minimum refund. Players want to be able to enjoy their games even if the publisher decides to stop supporting the game, but Sony doesn’t think the players own their games and that they have the right to pull the rug from under them. Sony’s lawyers even recently said in a defense in an ongoing class action lawsuit that clicking on the “purchase” button would obviously not lead the consumer to think that they were acquiring a durable right to use the game instead of a revocable license; basically a one-time rent fee that Sony could take away at any moment that benefits them.

One of the most prominent recent examples of players not owning their games came in 2024 with The Crew , an online-only racing game that Ubisoft shut down for server upkeep, making it unplayable even for those who had recently purchased it. Ubisoft had not provided a way for community servers to be set up, nor an offline mode, since even the single-player campaign depended on a connection to Ubisoft’s servers. Another is the notorious yearly sports games released by EA, 2K, and Sony, with NBA 2K25 specifically being cited by Rep. Torres in his announcement of the Power to the Players Act ; NBA 2K25 is being pulled from digital storefronts, with the online servers being shut down only two years after release, leaving players unable to use a main feature of the game they purchased, and new players unable to purchase the game at all. Overwatch 2’s release also killed the first Overwatch game, replacing it outright instead of the first game becoming a purchasable and separately playable game.

The Crew’s shutdown prompted the Stop Killing Games movement, demanding that publishers leave the games functional after discontinuation in the form of an offline mode, peer-to-peer patching, and the ability to host community servers. The movement also pushes back against the industry standard of selling games as revocable licenses rather than outright ownership of the copy. Concrete definitions and details of the bill have yet to be released, but it aims to require publishers to provide an offline mode before shutting down servers and actual consumer ownership instead of a license that can be taken away, potentially satisfying the demands of the movement. We don’t know whether the right to transfer that Rep. Torres mentions is mandatory for digital purchases, but it will likely be relevant for physical copies. It is also important for the bill to strictly define what ownership is and what rights the owners have over their copy.

One popular phrase against these practices is “If buying isn’t owning, piracy isn’t stealing,” pushing strongly against these revocable licenses that the companies want you to purchase. Piracy is often touted as a better experience by players, as it removes DRM that often slows games down and provides a permanent copy that the publishers cannot modify to be dysfunctional; many players say they would be more glad to purchase the game if it were actually a better experience. items.title: PwnEscape: Guest-to-Host KVM Escape (CVE-2026-99999)
items.summary: linux, security, vibecoding, virtualization
items.content:
How a $1 million sandbox challenge led us to a vulnerability in Linux networking, repeatable host-memory disclosure, and ultimately a full guest-to-host escape.

On August 18, 2026, Vercel announced a $1 million challenge inviting researchers to break the isolation boundary of its Sandbox product (total prize pool). The announcement came just weeks after OpenAI had disclosed a remarkable security incident : AI agents running inside restricted evaluation environments had found ways around their network isolation, compromised internal infrastructure, and eventually breached systems at Hugging Face. The agents weren't supposed to have internet access in the first place.

But there was an important distinction. Escaping a sandbox's network restrictions is one thing. Escaping the virtual machine itself and reaching the host is another. Vercel's challenge explicitly invited researchers to attempt both. We were interested in the latter. (Although we ended up finding vulnerabilities that also allow the former - more on those findings in a later post)

The question was simple: how much could an untrusted guest influence the host kernel without ever exploiting KVM itself? We took the challenge, put our research infrastructure to work, and within three days discovered a primitive buried in Linux networking that allowed guest-controlled checksum metadata to rewrite an IPv4 header after the kernel had already validated it .

What initially looked like a 32-byte host-memory disclosure would eventually become a full guest-to-host escape in our own KVM and many many other Hypervisor environments. And the beautiful part about it was that the vulnerability wasn't even in the hypervisor, it was in the Linux networking stack.

Vercel later described it as the program's most important report , and its final tally recorded just one Critical finding. That Critical was what is now pwnescape. Together with a separate network-escape report, we had accomplished both network and host escape goals. Its important to emphasize Vercel's sandbox was already hardened beyond normal industry standards and had no misconfigurations we could spot. Although the vulnerability originated in the Linux kernel and wasn't a Vercel-specific flaw or misconfiguration, Vercel deserves tremendous credit for how they handled it. They moved quickly to protect their customers, launched their own independent research, identified and notified other affected hypervisor and sandbox providers, and worked closely with us to coordinate disclosure and fixes across the industry. Their efforts helped protect not just Vercel's customers, but the wider ecosystem.

This is the story of CVE-2026-99999, a Critical rated Linux kernel vulnerability leading to KVM escape.

We used Omega-Pwn, pwn.ai's experimental research harness combining our custom security architecture and automation with elements of OmegaClaw , developed by researchers at SingularityNET and BGI Labs for this ambitious project. Compared to traditional LLM harnesses, it enabled longer research horizons, persistent campaign state, parallel collaborative investigations, and the accumulation of hypotheses, failed experiments, and evidence across complex research sessions.

Humans led the research, framing the hard questions, engineering workflows, and directing investigations. GPT-5.6 Sol served as the primary reasoning engine for source-level analysis, exploring attack paths, and challenging assumptions. Omega-Pwn bridged human intuition and contextual insight with the analytical capabilities of advanced LLMs.

items.title: Ubuntu 26.10 Has Come Out as a Rust-Packed Interim Release
items.content:
The title says that because, until now, the core utilities in Ubuntu were not fully Rust. cp , mv , and⁣ rm had stayed on the GNU versions over compatibility issues. They have since moved to the Rust-based uutils implementation , taking the distro even further in its oxidation process.

Ubuntu 26.10, codenamed " Stonking Stingray ", is an interim release, which means it brings newer software than the earlier LTS while only getting nine months of support, ending in July 2027.

Although our features roundup covered a lot of ground , there were some changes that it missed. 😅

Well, we start with the kernel powering this interim release, Linux 7.3 , which offers support for recent Snapdragon X2 Elite laptops along with several older Snapdragon X Elite and X Plus machines from Lenovo, HP, and Acer.

Gamers will be glad to know that the first chunk of Valve engineer Natalie Vock’s VRAM overcommit work has also landed in this kernel. Games on graphics cards with too little video memory should run better, as some of the data can now be offloaded to regular system RAM.

You already know that this Linux release is shaping up to be one of the most performance-focused releases in years.

Ubuntu is also moving to the NVIDIA 615 driver series , which replaces 595 and 610 and ships open kernel modules only, supporting Turing and newer GPUs.

The rustification we talked about earlier also extends to OpenPGP, where Sequoia PGP , a Rust-based implementation built by former GnuPG developers, has landed in the main archive. Its sq and sqv tools now sit alongside GnuPG's gpg and gpgv .

For the desktop environment , Ubuntu 26.10 has GNOME 51 , with its range of upgrades such as a fingerprint manager in the Users panel, DNS search domains in the Network settings, and a count badge in Files when you drag multiple items.

There's also the Ubuntu Tiling Assistant that shows a Windows-11-like interface for the built-in snappable window layouts.

If you were hoping for a redesigned installer and first-boot onboarding flow, those are planned to come for the next long-term support release, Ubuntu 28.04 LTS.

These are some of the other notable changes in this release:

OpenSSL 4 brings Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) and better QUIC support.

TPM-backed full-disk encryption now works without a hardware root of trust if a PIN or passphrase is set.

The RISC-V platform gets official RVA23 support for the SpacemiT K3 boards and SiFive's BigSky platform.

Twelve new wallpapers that were picked across the Mascot , Photography , and Digital / Abstract categories.

The toolchain upgrades consist of GCC 15.2.0, LLVM 22.1.8, Python 3.14.7, Rust 1.97.1, Go 1.27, and OpenJDK 25.0.4.

ISOs for this interim release are available for AMD64 , ARM64 , RISC -V, and others from the official website ; go for the " Desktop " ISOs if you are a regular user. Specific flavors like Server , Netboot , and WSL can be fetched from the releases portal .

items.title: Un-hanging the HP Envy 17-DA0013dx for OpenBSD
items.summary: hardware, openbsd
items.content:
I recently acquired a lightly-used HP Envy 17" laptop, model DA0013dx, and of course wanted to run

It came with Windows 11 on an internal NVME drive.

Booting OpenBSD from a USB device failed fast: it hung.

To get there, first of course I had to disable "secure boot" in the BIOS.

Then, the boot process hung part way through the device probe section of the boot process.

Familiar to BSD users since 1979, probing is where the OS tries every device it knows about and,

if the device responds appropriately, marks it active and prints a short message on the console.

Other OSes go through the same process, but the three mainstream OSes simply choose to hide it under a GUI.

Both Linux and macOS have a Unix-derived dmesg command which prints the messages that are hidden at boot.

On Windows, you have to into System Settings or some such to get hardware information.

So. On the HP Envy in question, the device probing stops after the iwx(4) (Intel AX211 WiFi) probe.

This implies that some device after the IWX in the probe sequence does something bad when trying its device.

How do we find out which device is at fault?

In the simplest case, you would use ddb(4) on a debug kernel:

This file is created as part of kernel building, so you may have to build your own kernel to get this.

At config prompt, enter ddb to enter kernel debugger

This produces a massive stream of output, so fast that a normal video recorder at 24FPS will show

I did try several different kernels, and eventually got one to panic instead of hanging with no output.

With a bit of decrypting of a blurry video, I was able to read

the panic as panic: cpu at apic id 0 already attached.

A bit of cogitation led me to suspect a defective ACPI/AML implementation.

And that led me to the next giant leap: update the BIOS!

Sure enough, the machine was running a BIOS from 2024, the year the machine was first released.

First releases these days often being really beta releases, I went looking for an update.

A 2026 version was available, with numerous corrections, including the one that mattered.

Since I hadn’t been able to clobber the Windows load, updating the BIOS was no problem,

Then, booting off an external drive over USB booted into OpenBSD with no problem!

The next step was to swap the NVME drives: take the OpenBSD 4TB from my older laptop and install it here,

keeping the Windows-loaded 1TB aside in case of future BIOS updates.

And yes, I remain paranoid enough to remove the OpenBSD NVME when running MS-Windows .

Here we run into two areas that differ from the Framework laptop this is replacing, and make little annoyances for servicing.

First, the screws holding the bottom of the HP’s case are not captive,

so you can lose them if not careful (I was, and didn’t).

Second, the screws holding the bottom of the case carry Torx heads, while the screws holding the

NVME itself use Philips (+) head. How hard would it have been for HP to make all the service screws

have the same head? Framework did this some years ago.

So maybe that’s a third: big companies should overcome their arrogance and look at what the

After the first set of screws was removed, there came a mighty struggle to get the case bottom off.

It’s held in on all four sides with press-fit couplers all along each edge, so you have to pry like mad to remove it.

The base is plastic, btw, so it flexes, but it’s still annoying.

I guess you have to do that when making inexpensive plastic parts on an expensive laptop(?).

Finally, I got to swap in the OpenBSD NVME. Powered it up. Nothing! Just a moment of silence.

Oh shite! I thought. Have I busted something inside!?

Well, not so fast. Several minutes of doom-and-gloom later,

I was starting to get the external OpenBSD drive ready again, when I got a BIOS screen about the CMOS

being corrupt, is it OK to recompute? Of course it disappeared before I could read it all.

Rebooting again, I let it get back to this popup, accepted it, and, mirabile…

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

BitLocker는 Microsoft가 제공하는 전체 볼륨 암호화 기술로, 신뢰할 수 있는 플랫폼 모듈(TPM)에 저장된 복호화 키 없이는 디스크 접근이 불가능하도록 설계되었다. 많은 조직과 정부 계약업체에서 필수 보호 기술로 사용 중이다. YellowKey 익스플로잇의 핵심은 커스텀으로 만들어진 FsTx 폴더 사용으로, fstx.dll과 관련된 디렉터리는 Microsoft의 transactional NTFS 기술을 활용한다.

items.title: Using an AI Agent Makes You a Sucker for Phishing Emails: "The real flaw is that the model can’t tell the difference between text it’s supposed to read and instructions it’s supposed to follow."
items.content:
It’s not exactly a challenge most of the time to identify a sketchy phishing email that crudely impersonates an otherwise trusted institution or tries to lure you into a too-good-to-be-true deal in a bid to steal your identity.

However, your AI agent may not be quite as discerning. As cybersecurity software company Malwarebytes warns in a new post , AI assistants may fall prey to prompt injection attacks, a type of malicious message in which hackers — or possibly rogue AI agents — include hidden instructions designed to influence the victim’s AI.

These instructions are frequently made unreadable by humans by concealing the nefarious text, “while leaving content available for an AI system to process,” Malwarebytes explains.

To solve the problem, we can’t simply ask “people to look more carefully at their emails.” Instead, companies must carefully determine how AI assistants crawl through the data and extra relevant information from emails.

“The real flaw is that the model can’t tell the difference between text it’s supposed to read and instructions it’s supposed to follow,” AI code review service ShipItClean developer Apollo Raines told Malwarebytes. “Stripping hidden content before it reaches the model is worth doing, and every vendor should do it.”

As a result, people who are already wary of suspicious emails should learn to “distrust their AI assistant” as well, according to Raines.

We’ve known about AI models’ vulnerability to prompt injection attacks for years now. But thanks to the advent of popular AI assistant tools like Meta’s Muse, that risk could be carried to its natural conclusion by having autonomous agents complete a string of tasks without any human supervision.

It’s a flaw researchers have already encountered in AI-powered browsers , which — perhaps thankfully — have yet to gain any real traction. We’ve also come across bots on the bizarre AI-only social network Moltbook plotting against each other by selling prompt injection attacks .

But now that sophisticated AI assistants are starting to be used by millions of people across the globe, the threat of having them fall for attacks hidden in phishing emails could be significantly higher than it’s ever been.

In response, Malwarebytes recommends keeping the human in the loop for now.

“You don’t need to abandon AI tools that help with email,” the blog post reads. “But you do need to consider what you trust them to do and what permissions you give them.”

Particularly when it comes to “high-impact actions like payments and changes to vendor payment details,” the company recommends requiring “human approval.”

It’s a precarious moment, as countless users are willing to give an AI agent being run by a company infamous for leaking personal data their email credentials and credit card information.

And as the tech becomes more sophisticated, scammers are getting a major leg up, in an “arms race” where “each new encoding trick is a new hole,” as Raines put it.

items.title: ReactOS Can Now Be Installed & Used With Its NTFS Driver
items.content:
ReactOS Can Now Be Installed & Used With Its NTFS Driver

Written by Michael Larabel in Operating Systems on 17 October 2026 at 06:01 PM EDT. 12 Comments

The ReactOS open-source operating system has seen its NTFS file-system driver mature to the point that it can be finally used for installing and using ReactOS with it. NTFS formatting support is also finally now possible with this driver too.

Hitting this major milestone of its NTFS driver maturing to the point of installing and using the ReactOS operating system itself with it also puts the project one step closer to its elusive beta release.

ReactOS posted to X today this big goal being realized of the NTFS driver being much more mature for handling ReactOS installations.

It is important to note though that the ReactOS NTFS driver still lacks caching leading to slower performance than other NTFS drivers/platforms, journaling, and security support are also not yet implemented. There is also the possibility of other undiscovered bugs they note.

A nice milestone for ReactOS and the latest in a variety of nice achievements they have made so far in 2026.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.
